strengths: The paper addresses a practical bottleneck in visual autoregressive generation. Restricting cross-scale dependencies and using neighborhood attention is a plausible approach to reducing memory while preserving generation quality.

The reported results show a promising quality–efficiency tradeoff: the 310M model improves ImageNet-256 FID from 3.55 to 3.09, while fine-tuned models report 2.8–3.2× lower inference memory and modest latency improvements.
The ablations examine conditioning-history length, neighborhood size, and the incremental contributions of both components. Appendix C provides useful training and sampling hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The efficiency evaluation contains a significant hardware inconsistency. Table 2 states that all measurements use an RTX 4090, but reports successful training with memory footprints of 27,665–48,173 MB, exceeding its 24 GB capacity. The hardware, memory accounting, and any distributed execution or offloading must be clarified before the central training-efficiency claims can be trusted.

The claimed Markov factorization is insufficiently specified. The paper retains VAR's residual tokenizer, but Equation 1 subtracts only the previous residual token map rather than explicitly defining the cumulative reconstruction. It is unclear whether conditioning uses the previous residual map or an accumulated representation containing earlier scales. These imply different conditional-independence claims. The construction and resizing of inputs for Equations 3–7 also need an explicit algorithm.

The complexity comparison is partly incorrect. Appendix B assigns O(i²) cost to attention between the current token and i−1 previous tokens, yielding O(N³) for next-token generation. With standard KV caching, this attention costs O(i) per step and O(N²) overall. The proposed O(Nk) attention bound is plausible, but comparisons must use consistent caching assumptions and distinguish attention cost from total model computation.

The quality comparisons do not isolate the architectural contribution adequately. Fine-tuned MVAR receives 80 additional epochs, without a VAR control receiving equivalent continued training. The from-scratch comparison uses official pretrained VAR weights rather than a clearly matched training recipe. FID gains for the larger models are small, and all fine-tuned variants reduce recall; d20 and d24 also reduce IS. These results support a tradeoff more than uniform superiority.

Novelty and competitive positioning remain underdeveloped. Neighborhood attention is established prior work, explicitly cited as references 13–14. Closely related efficient VAR methods, including FastVAR and collaborative decoding, are cited but not compared experimentally. Consequently, the paper does not establish whether its combination offers a compelling advantage over existing efficiency techniques.

Attention concentration motivates pruning but does not establish conditional independence or information redundancy. Aggregated attention mass can also reflect different token counts across scales. Controlled interventions or predictive-loss measurements would better support the Markov interpretation. Moreover, stacking local-attention layers expands the effective receptive field beyond a single k-token neighborhood.

Evaluation is limited to class-conditional ImageNet at 256×256, leaving the claimed scaling benefits untested at higher resolutions. The manuscript does not clearly specify evaluation sample counts, uncertainty across runs, or the profiling protocol. The component ablations use only a shortened 50-epoch schedule and omit a spatial-only variant, limiting confidence in the full-training contribution of each component.

strengths: Addresses a practical limitation of visual autoregressive generation: memory consumption. Restricting scale dependencies and using neighborhood attention is a plausible, implementable approach.
Reports substantial inference-memory reductions of 2.8–3.2× across three model sizes, with modest latency improvements and comparable FID.

The 310M model trained from scratch improves FID from 3.55 to 3.09. Component and neighborhood-size ablations provide useful evidence that both restrictions can preserve or improve generation quality.
weaknesses: The conditioning state is insufficiently specified for the central Markov claim. VAR uses cumulative reconstructions of residual codes, whereas Equation 1 subtracts only the preceding residual map. The paper must clarify whether MVAR conditions on an individual residual map or an accumulated reconstruction; the latter still contains information from earlier scales. The alignment between differently sized scales and the construction of transformer inputs are also unclear.

The training-efficiency results contain a significant hardware inconsistency. Table 2 states that all measurements use an RTX 4090, but reports successful training with 27,665–48,173 MB of memory, exceeding that GPU's 24 GB capacity. Different hardware, aggregation, offloading, or estimated measurements would require explicit disclosure before these results can be interpreted.

Fine-tuning comparisons are not compute-matched: MVAR receives 80 additional epochs, but there is no VAR control continued for the same duration. Consequently, the small FID improvements cannot be attributed confidently to the proposed architecture. Recall decreases for every fine-tuned model, and IS decreases for d20 and d24, weakening claims of superior overall quality.

Novelty and competitive efficiency are not adequately established. Spatial-Markov attention directly uses existing neighborhood-attention ideas, while the evaluation omits relevant efficient VAR methods cited by the paper, including FastVAR and collaborative decoding. Comparisons against these approaches are more informative than many of the older generation baselines.

Attention concentration motivates pruning but does not establish conditional independence or dispensability. Accumulated attention weights are affected by scale size, and hidden features can carry earlier-scale information. The paper lacks controlled intervention or likelihood evidence supporting its stronger interpretation of the attention visualizations.

The complexity analysis mischaracterizes cached token-wise autoregressive inference as O(N³): with KV caching, attention costs O(i) at step i and O(N²) overall. The proposed O(Nk) attention scaling is plausible, but it should be distinguished from whole-model cost and supported by resolution-scaling measurements.

Evaluation is restricted to ImageNet 256×256, with no higher-resolution validation of the principal scalability claim. Sampling counts, uncertainty estimates, and sufficiently detailed baseline sampling settings are missing; ablations use only a shortened 50-epoch schedule. These gaps limit confidence in small quality differences and broader applicability.

strengths: Addresses a practical bottleneck in visual autoregressive generation: memory consumption from attending across scales. Combining adjacent-scale conditioning with neighborhood attention is a simple, useful architectural direction.

Reports substantial inference-memory reductions of 2.8–3.2× across three model sizes, alongside modest latency improvements. The 310M model trained from scratch improves ImageNet-256 FID from 3.55 to 3.09.

Provides informative ablations on conditioning history and neighborhood size. The scale-only variant improves FID from 4.84 to 4.35, with neighborhood attention further improving it to 4.16 under the reported abbreviated training schedule.
Includes training and sampling hyperparameters, attention visualizations, and qualitative examples that help explain the approach.
weaknesses: The hardware measurements contain a major unresolved inconsistency. Table 2 states that all experiments use an RTX 4090, but reports training-memory consumption of 34,319–48,173 MB for VAR and 27,665–38,579 MB for larger MVAR models, exceeding that GPU’s 24 GB capacity. Training times are nevertheless reported for several such configurations. The paper must clarify whether these measurements are aggregate, estimated, offloaded, or obtained on different hardware before its training-efficiency claims can be assessed.

The implemented conditioning state is insufficiently specified. Equation 4 conditions on only the preceding residual token map, whereas standard VAR inputs incorporate accumulated residual reconstructions. Equation 1 also omits the cumulative residual subtraction expected in that tokenizer. The paper needs to distinguish a genuinely Markov model over residual tokens from attention pruning over a state that already summarizes earlier scales, and explicitly describe resampling and transformer inputs.

The quality comparisons do not adequately isolate the proposed modifications. Fine-tuned MVAR receives 80 additional epochs without an equally fine-tuned VAR control. Matched training and sampling settings for the scratch comparison are not established clearly. Moreover, Table 2 shows reduced recall at every model size and lower IS for d20 and d24, so broad claims of superior performance obscure fidelity–diversity tradeoffs.

Novelty and competitive efficiency remain insufficiently established. Neighborhood attention is an existing mechanism explicitly adopted here, while closely related efficient VAR approaches, including the cited FastVAR and collaborative decoding methods, receive no quantitative comparison. Comparisons against these methods and an optimized VAR implementation are needed to establish the value of the combination.

The theoretical motivation overinterprets attention concentration as conditional independence. Attention mass alone does not establish that discarded information is redundant, and accumulated weights across differently sized scales require careful normalization. Appendix B also incorrectly assigns O(i²) work to a current-token attention query over i cached tokens; conventional cached autoregressive attention totals O(N²), rather than the claimed O(N³).

Evaluation is restricted to ImageNet at 256×256, without empirical resolution scaling to substantiate the broader linear-complexity advantage. Reported FLOPs cover attention blocks rather than the full model, and sample counts, uncertainty estimates, and detailed memory/timing protocols are missing. These gaps are particularly consequential for the small FID improvements in the fine-tuning experiments.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical bottleneck in visual autoregressive generation. Restricting scale dependencies and using neighborhood attention offers a simple, potentially useful way to reduce memory consumption.

Reported results show promising quality–efficiency tradeoffs: scratch-trained MVAR-d16 improves ImageNet-256 FID from 3.55 to 3.09, while the fine-tuned variants report approximately threefold lower inference memory with comparable FID.

The evaluation includes component ablations, conditioning-history length, neighborhood size, and training schedules. Appendix experiments extend coverage to ImageNet-512, face datasets, and a 2B-parameter model.
weaknesses: The hardware and memory measurements are inconsistent as documented. Table 2 claims measurements on an RTX 4090 yet reports successful training runs requiring 27–48 GB; Tables 6–7 similarly report approximately 42–48 GB despite a standard RTX 4090 having 24 GB. Aggregation across devices, modified hardware, offloading, or estimated measurements are not explained. Because memory efficiency is the central contribution, this substantially undermines confidence in the evaluation.

The claimed Markov factorization is insufficiently connected to the implementation. VAR uses accumulated multiscale reconstructions as conditioning features, whereas Eq. (4) conditions only on the preceding residual token map. The paper does not clearly specify whether MVAR retains accumulated features or uses only the last residual. Retaining accumulated features preserves information from earlier scales; using only the last residual requires an explicit construction that is missing. Equations (3)–(7) also do not adequately explain alignment between adjacent resolutions or the actual source of queries, keys, and values.

Attention concentration does not establish conditional independence. Averaging attention over heads and layers can obscure important long-range dependencies, and stacked neighborhood-attention layers expand the effective receptive field beyond a single neighborhood. The empirical results support useful attention restrictions, but not the stronger probabilistic interpretation asserted in the paper.

Training-efficiency comparisons are not sufficiently controlled. Appendix D.5 reveals that mixed training updates different scale groups on different iterations, so seconds per iteration do not represent equivalent work relative to VAR's all-scale updates. The main experiments do not clearly identify the selected ratio, loss weighting, or effective exposure of each scale. End-to-end training time and compute to matched quality are needed. Likewise, the fine-tuning comparison lacks a VAR control receiving the same additional 80 epochs.

Positioning against relevant efficiency methods is weak. FastVAR and collaborative decoding are cited but not evaluated, while spatial-Markov attention directly adopts established neighborhood attention. Comparisons primarily against vanilla VAR do not establish that this combination advances the quality–memory–latency frontier beyond existing efficient VAR approaches.

The complexity discussion contains an error: Appendix A assigns O(i²) cost to attending from the current token to i preceding tokens and concludes O(N³) for next-token generation. With KV caching, that attention computation is O(i), giving O(N²) total attention cost. The proposed O(Nk) attention bound is plausible for fixed neighborhoods, but attention-only FLOPs should be distinguished from total model computation and measured end-to-end gains.

Evaluation details and claims need tightening. Main-result FID sample counts, reference statistics, and uncertainty are unspecified; small fine-tuning gains are accompanied by consistently lower recall. The statement that MVAR outperforms nearly all competing models is contradicted by several lower-FID entries in Table 1. The appendix also describes CelebA as containing 30,000 images without explaining the subset or dataset variant, making those experiments difficult to reproduce.

strengths: Addresses a practically important limitation of visual autoregressive generation: memory consumption. Restricting scale dependencies and using neighborhood attention is a plausible approach, with reported inference-memory reductions of approximately 3×.
Reports encouraging quality–efficiency tradeoffs: the scratch-trained ImageNet-256 model improves FID from 3.55 to 3.09, while larger fine-tuned models retain competitive quality.

Includes useful component ablations, conditioning-history and neighborhood-size sweeps, and supplementary experiments on ImageNet-512, CelebA, and FFHQ. The appendix also examines the mixed-training schedule.
weaknesses: The hardware measurements contain major unresolved inconsistencies. Table 2 reports training memory of 34,319–48,173 MB while stating experiments used an RTX 4090, ordinarily a 24 GB GPU. Tables 6–7 similarly report approximately 42–48 GB under single-4090 captions. Modified hardware, aggregation across devices, or offloading could explain this, but none is specified. Because memory efficiency is the central contribution, the measurement protocol and hardware must be clarified.

The claimed Markov factorization is insufficiently specified. The manuscript defines r_l as a residual token map, whereas VAR normally constructs next-scale inputs from accumulated reconstructions of earlier residuals. It does not clearly establish whether MVAR conditions on only the preceding residual or on a cumulative feature representation. The latter retains earlier-scale information and changes the interpretation of Equation 4. Cross-resolution alignment and the sources of queries, keys, and values also need explicit definition.

Attention concentration motivates pruning but does not establish conditional independence. Averaging attention across heads and layers can hide important long-range dependencies; stacked neighborhood attention also expands the effective receptive field beyond one k-token neighborhood. The paper overinterprets these observations as evidence for its probabilistic factorization.

The quality comparisons do not fully isolate the proposed changes. Table 2 gives MVAR 80 additional fine-tuning epochs without a matched continued-training VAR control. Its small FID improvements also accompany lower recall at every model size and lower IS for d20/d24, weakening claims of overall superiority. Repeated runs or uncertainty estimates are absent.

Novelty and competitive efficiency remain insufficiently established. Neighborhood attention is an existing mechanism explicitly adopted here, and the principal additional change is restriction of scale history. Despite citing FastVAR and collaborative decoding, the paper provides no direct comparisons with these closely related efficiency methods or controlled comparisons against alternative cache-reduction approaches.

The complexity analysis incorrectly assigns O(N³) to standard next-token generation without distinguishing uncached recomputation from KV-cached decoding, whose attention cost is O(N²). Training speed is reported per iteration even though mixed training changes which scales are processed; matched-work throughput and total time to comparable quality are needed.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the hyperparameter table. The main generation evaluations do not clearly specify sample counts and reference statistics, the default mixed-training ratio and loss weighting are unclear, and the stated 30,000-image CelebA dataset needs identification as a subset or CelebA-HQ. Code and checkpoints are promised rather than supplied.

strengths: Addresses a practically important bottleneck in visual autoregressive generation: attention computation and KV-cache memory. Combining restricted scale conditioning with neighborhood attention is a plausible efficiency strategy.
Reports encouraging ImageNet results: MVAR-d16 improves FID from 3.55 to 3.09, while fine-tuned variants report approximately 2.8–3.2× lower inference memory and modest latency improvements.

Includes useful component ablations covering conditioning history, neighborhood size, and mixed-training ratios. Appendix experiments extend evaluation to 512×512 generation, face datasets, and a 2B-parameter model.
Provides training and sampling hyperparameters, qualitative examples, and attention visualizations that help explain the proposed design.
weaknesses: The central memory measurements conflict with the stated hardware. Table 2 reports successful training using 34,319–48,173 MB on an RTX 4090, which normally has 24 GB of memory; Tables 6–7 likewise report successful runs exceeding this capacity. Modified hardware, aggregation across devices, or offloading could explain these numbers, but none is specified. This substantially undermines the reproducibility and interpretation of the primary efficiency claim.

The claimed Markov factorization is insufficiently connected to the implementation. The paper defines r_l as residual tokens, but does not clearly specify whether the next-scale input contains only the preceding residual or the accumulated reconstruction used by VAR. Accumulated features would retain information from earlier scales despite removing their attention cache. Equation 1 also omits the usual accumulation over earlier residual contributions. Explicit state definitions and training/inference pseudocode are needed to establish what conditional independence is actually imposed.

Quality comparisons are not adequately controlled. Table 2 compares MVAR after 80 additional fine-tuning epochs against unchanged pretrained VAR, without an equally fine-tuned VAR control. In addition, recall decreases for every fine-tuned variant and IS decreases for d20/d24, so the claim of broadly superior performance overstates the evidence. Matched training budgets and sampling-parameter sweeps would better distinguish architectural improvements from additional training and fidelity–diversity tradeoffs.

Novelty and competitive efficiency are insufficiently established. Neighborhood attention is an existing technique explicitly reused here, and the paper cites relevant efficient-VAR approaches, including FastVAR and collaborative decoding, without comparing against them. Comparisons primarily against vanilla VAR do not establish whether the proposed combination offers a competitive quality–memory–latency tradeoff.

The complexity discussion contains an error: Appendix A assigns O(i²) cost to attending from the current token to i−1 preceding tokens and consequently claims O(N³) next-token generation. With KV caching, that attention costs O(i), yielding O(N²) overall. The O(Nk) neighborhood-attention bound is plausible under the stated assumptions, but should be separated from full-model computation and supported by resolution-scaling measurements.

Important evaluation details remain unclear: the default mixed-training ratio and loss weighting, comparable work per reported training iteration, and main-table FID sample counts/reference statistics are not specified adequately. The CelebA description also states 30,000 images without identifying the subset or variant. These gaps, together with the unresolved measurement inconsistencies, prevent the otherwise promising results from meeting the acceptance threshold.
